task.goal: Diagnose intermittent vibration in one of six identical ventilation fans before a planned maintenance shutdown.
hard_constraints: A mechanic has one week, a handheld vibration meter, existing maintenance logs and one 30-minute shutdown window.
Do not open energized housings or stop all ventilation simultaneously.
Distinguish imbalance, loose mounting and bearing wear without claiming a cause from one noisy measurement; state a safe escalation trigger.
task.available_resources: Five healthy fans as comparators and a spare mounting kit.
task.expected_result: A prioritized diagnostic sequence and repair decision.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Matched-condition comparison before targeted shutdown inspection
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: distinguish a persistent mechanical signature from operating-condition effects by repeatedly comparing the suspect fan with the five healthy units. Assumptions: external bearing supports and mounting points are safely accessible, operating conditions can be identified, and the meter supports repeatable readings. Frequency or bearing-condition features are optional; a basic overall-value meter cannot reliably separate imbalance from bearing wear alone.

During the first four days, review logs for onset, prior bearing or mounting work, and links to speed or ventilation demand. Measure all six fans at equivalent external locations, in the same directions, using consistent meter contact and settings. Repeat across several operating periods, recording load or speed when available. Prioritize inspection when the suspect repeatedly exceeds the healthy range under comparable conditions. Strong radial vibration with a rotational-frequency component, if measurable, supports imbalance; visible mounting movement or inconsistent directional response supports looseness; bearing-localized vibration, roughness, or supported high-frequency indications support bearing wear. None establishes a cause alone.

Use the 30-minute window to isolate and lock out only the suspect fan, after confirming the remaining ventilation is adequate. Prioritize external mounting inspection, then accessible bearing play and roughness checks, then safe visual inspection for blade damage or deposits. Install the spare mounting kit only where compatible and warranted, using specified torque. Do not attempt unsupported balancing or a rushed bearing replacement. If evidence favors imbalance or bearing wear, arrange the appropriate specialist repair.

Escalate immediately under site procedures for rapid worsening, severe knocking, visible structural movement, rubbing, or an applicable equipment alarm limit. Stop and isolate the affected fan when required; preserve other ventilation. Missing limits or inconsistent evidence require engineering review rather than a confident diagnosis.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Smallest check: repeat matched readings on the suspect and one healthy fan before and after any repair, at unchanged locations and comparable operation. If their ranges overlap or the suspected signature does not repeat, the initial diagnosis is unsupported. Improvement after mounting repair supports a mounting contribution; persistent vibration requires further investigation. Record uncertainty and retain both comparison records.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use the shutdown as a controlled mounting intervention
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: use a documented mounting correction as a causal intervention, rather than relying chiefly on vibration signatures. This is useful when the handheld meter measures only overall vibration. Prerequisites are a compatible spare mounting kit, approved mounting and torque instructions, safe external measurement points, and confirmation that five operating fans can maintain required ventilation. The method can identify a mounting contribution but cannot conclusively distinguish imbalance from bearing wear without additional evidence.

Early in the week, review maintenance logs and collect repeated suspect-fan readings alongside one healthy comparator, checking the other healthy fans to establish normal variation. Keep measurement position, direction, settings, and operating condition consistent. Document externally visible mounting defects without touching moving parts or opening energized housings. Prepare tools, kit, isolation arrangements, and a time-limited work plan before the shutdown.

During the single 30-minute window, isolate and lock out only the suspect fan. First inspect and document mounting condition. Check accessible bearing roughness or play and inspect the rotor for deposits, damage, or rubbing where safely possible. If a mounting defect is present, correct it with the spare kit and specified torque. Avoid unrelated adjustments so the intervention remains interpretable. If mounting is sound, do not replace it merely to create an experiment: use the remaining time for inspection and plan the indicated repair. Restore guards before restart; leave the fan isolated if safe restoration cannot be completed.

A sustained reduction after correction supports looseness as a contributor. Residual vibration associated with rotor deposits or damage favors an imbalance investigation; bearing roughness or abnormal play favors bearing service. Either can coexist with looseness. Inconclusive residual vibration warrants specialist diagnostics, not a forced choice.

Escalate immediately for rapid vibration growth, severe knocking, rubbing, structural movement, or an applicable alarm limit. Follow site isolation procedures while maintaining the other ventilation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare several pre-intervention and post-intervention readings with the unchanged healthy fan under matched operation. A reduction larger than ordinary repeat variation, sustained on subsequent checks, supports the mounting hypothesis. No reduction weakens mounting as the principal cause. A simultaneous change in the healthy comparator suggests operating-condition confounding; defer the repair conclusion until matched readings are available.

EXPAND.title: Use the shutdown to separate local vibration from transmitted vibration
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: remove the suspect fan’s excitation while the other five continue running. Vibration that persists on its stationary support suggests transmission through the structure; a substantial decrease supports a source associated with the suspect fan, without identifying the defect alone. This addresses a gap in matched running comparisons: identical fans can share structural vibration.

The mechanic owns the one-week trial. First review logs and establish repeat readings at safely accessible external bearing supports and the adjacent fixed frame, including comparable points on healthy fans. Record operating conditions and measurement variation. Prepare approved isolation procedures, inspection tools and the compatible mounting kit. Confirm that five fans can maintain required ventilation; otherwise obtain an approved ventilation arrangement before proceeding.

During the single 30-minute window, stop and lock out only the suspect fan. After complete standstill, repeat readings at the same external points while the others run steadily. Then inspect mounting interfaces, accessible bearing play or roughness, and safely accessible rotor deposits or damage. Never open an energized housing. Reserve time to restore guards and check safe operation.

Persistent stationary vibration redirects investigation toward the supporting structure or another operating fan; it does not exclude a local defect. A large decrease plus defective mounting supports mounting repair with specified torque. Sound mounting plus rotor deposits or damage supports an imbalance investigation. Bearing roughness or excessive play supports bearing service. Mixed or weak evidence requires specialist diagnosis. Perform only a warranted mounting repair that fits the window; otherwise document and hand off.

Escalate immediately for rapid worsening, severe knocking, rubbing, visible structural movement or an applicable equipment limit. Isolate the affected fan under site procedures, preserving ventilation. Leave it isolated if safe restoration is incomplete.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare running, stationary and restored-operation readings against repeat variation and one continuously operating healthy fan. Against ordinary matched comparisons, success means resolving a previously ambiguous source without consuming the inspection reserve. Stop the extra measurements if access is unsafe or the reserved restoration time is reached. If stationary readings are negligible and the repair decision is unchanged, source isolation added work without diagnostic benefit.

EXPAND.title: Test whether airflow loading triggers the intermittent vibration
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: use a reversible change in an existing, approved airflow control to test whether aerodynamic loading triggers the vibration. This can prevent mistaking an operating-condition problem for imbalance or bearing wear. It requires independently adjustable existing controls, permission under normal operating procedures, and sufficient ventilation throughout. If those prerequisites are absent, this route is unsuitable.

The mechanic begins by reviewing logs for vibration episodes associated with damper position, demand changes or parallel-fan operation. Establish repeat external bearing-support and mounting readings on the suspect and healthy fans. Select two already permitted airflow settings at unchanged fan speed, where possible. Change only the suspect fan’s existing control, keeping all six fans running and maintaining required airflow. Use a short A–B–A sequence, recording settings and comparator readings. Do not improvise restrictions or enter moving equipment. Reappearance at the original setting makes a loading relationship more credible than a single high reading; it still does not establish the underlying defect.

Use the one 30-minute shutdown to isolate and lock out only the suspect fan. Inspect mounts, accessible bearing play and roughness, and safely accessible rotor condition. Restore guards before restart. Correct documented mounting defects with the compatible spare kit and specified torque if time permits. Bearing defects warrant bearing service; rotor damage or deposits warrant an imbalance investigation. A repeatable loading response with sound accessible mechanical checks warrants airflow/system review before balancing or bearing replacement. Mechanical defects and aerodynamic excitation can coexist.

Resume only within approved operating conditions. The mechanic hands off unresolved findings with readings, settings and inspection evidence. Stop the trial and escalate under site procedures for rapid growth, severe knocking, rubbing, structural movement, equipment-limit exceedance or inadequate ventilation; isolate the affected fan when required.
EXPAND.experiment: Bound the first trial to one short A–B–A sequence before shutdown. Compare its repair decision with the decision supported by matched-condition readings alone. A repeatable suspect-specific response supports pursuing airflow excitation; similar changes across healthy fans weaken that inference. Count added adjustment time and any ventilation disturbance against diagnostic benefit. Stop immediately if airflow requirements cannot be maintained. If the sequence adds no repeatable information, return to inspection-based diagnosis without further operational trials.

EXPAND.title: Upgrade: controlled mounting correction with an explicit intermittent-fault verification gate
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “Use the shutdown as a controlled mounting intervention.” This is the strongest practical route when the handheld meter provides only overall vibration: a warranted mounting correction supplies causal evidence without requiring a spectrum analyzer. The changed decision is that disappearance of an intermittent episode after repair cannot by itself close the diagnosis; verification must include comparable operating conditions, and worsening after repair triggers isolation and handoff.

During the week, the mechanic reviews logs for episode timing, operating conditions and previous repairs. Establish normal variation using equivalent external measurement points on all five healthy fans, then repeatedly measure the suspect and one healthy reference during comparable operation, including a reported episode if safely possible. Keep meter settings, contact position and direction consistent. Record actual readings and conditions. If no episode is captured, retain that uncertainty rather than treating ordinary readings as proof of health.

Prepare the compatible mounting kit, approved torque information, necessary tools and isolation arrangements before the single 30-minute shutdown. Confirm that the remaining fans can maintain required ventilation. The mechanic isolates and locks out only the suspect fan, verifies standstill and prevents unexpected movement under site procedures. Inspect and document mounting defects, accessible bearing play or roughness, and safely accessible rotor deposits, damage or rubbing. Never open an energized housing. Correct only a documented mounting defect that can be completed within the window; avoid unrelated adjustments. Reserve sufficient time for safe reassembly and restart checks. If safe completion is doubtful, leave the affected fan isolated and hand off under site procedures.

Repeated abnormal vibration plus a mounting defect and a sustained matched-condition reduction after correction supports looseness as a contributor. Accessible bearing roughness or excessive play supports bearing service. Sound mounts with rotor deposits or damage supports an imbalance investigation; visual condition alone does not prove imbalance. Mixed evidence can indicate multiple defects. With only overall vibration and inconclusive inspection, imbalance versus bearing wear remains unresolved and requires specialist diagnosis.

The mechanic performs only mounting work within their existing authorization. Bearing service or balancing is handed to the responsible maintenance person with readings, operating conditions, inspection findings and work performed. Escalate immediately for rapid growth, severe knocking, rubbing, visible structural movement, an applicable equipment limit or inadequate ventilation. If restart worsens vibration or reveals unsafe behavior, stop and isolate the affected fan under site procedures; do not consume the remaining window attempting repeated adjustments. Keep the other ventilation operating.
EXPAND.experiment: Use this fan and its single shutdown as the bounded trial. Compare repeated pre-correction suspect/reference readings with post-correction readings at the same locations and comparable conditions, including the conditions previously associated with episodes. Judge reduction against observed repeatability and healthy-fan variation, not an invented universal threshold. Compared with routine inspection and repair, the added burden is documenting comparable follow-up readings; it may prevent premature closure and an unnecessary bearing replacement or balancing job. No clear reduction, continuing episodes, or comparable changes on the healthy reference would show that the mounting intervention has not demonstrated useful diagnostic gain. If the triggering conditions do not recur within the week, report provisional improvement with diagnosis unresolved, and hand off the conditions needed for verification. Do not recreate an unsafe episode to complete the comparison.
